title: Rahul Gandhi says petrol has too much ethanol after Karnataka tests; oil companies reject findings
dek: Karnataka's government says lab tests found up to 31.2% ethanol in petrol meant to carry about 20%. Indian Oil, BPCL and HPCL say their fuel meets the standard and question how the samples were tested.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi on Saturday accused the Centre of letting motorists be short-changed on petrol, citing tests ordered by Karnataka's Congress government that it says found up to 31.2% ethanol in fuel sold as E20, which is meant to contain about 20%. The three state-run oil companies, Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum, have rejected the findings and questioned how the tests were done.

"E20 has turned into 420," Mr Gandhi wrote in a Hindi post on X, using the number of the old penal-code section on cheating, and called it "petrol theft" from people's cars. "Modi ji, tell us: what's being put in the country's tank? How much ethanol is actually in the petrol?" he wrote, according to an English rendering of the post.

## What Karnataka says

Karnataka's Department of Food, Civil Supplies, Consumer Affairs and Legal Metrology said on Friday that petrol at some outlets contained 26% to 31% ethanol, according to reports of its press release. Food and Civil Supplies Minister Rizwan Arshad said samples had been collected in October from outlets in seven districts: Bengaluru, Bengaluru Rural, Kolar, Chikkaballapura, Ramanagara, Tumakuru and Mangaluru, and tested at the Shriram Research Institute in Bengaluru, which reports describe as an accredited laboratory.

Mr Gandhi said 11 of 14 samples contained more than 20% ethanol, and that the highest readings were 31.2% at an Indian Oil outlet and 30.5% at an HPCL outlet. He said fuel from private retailers Nayara and Shell had also exceeded the limit. He criticised the absence of labels at fuel stations showing ethanol content, and repeated his challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi to a public debate. Karnataka minister G Parameshwara also called for an immediate investigation and asked the Prime Minister and Union minister Nitin Gadkari to explain.

## What the oil companies say

In a joint response on Friday, the three public-sector companies said E20 petrol across their networks, including in Karnataka, conforms to the Bureau of Indian Standards specification IS 17021, which allows 19% to 21% ethanol. They said the state's findings were "not supported by tests conducted in accordance with prescribed statutory and technical procedures", according to reports, and that the third-party lab certificates did not disclose enough about the method to verify the ethanol levels. They asked Karnataka for the full sampling records, lab reports and methodology, and proposed that the counterpart samples be retested using the prescribed referee method in the presence of state and company officials.

The Union Petroleum Ministry had not commented on the Karnataka findings by Saturday afternoon, and the BJP had not responded to Mr Gandhi's post.

## Background

India moved to 20% ethanol blending in petrol nationally in 2025, five years ahead of the original target, to cut oil imports and support sugarcane and grain farmers. The Petroleum Ministry says the programme has saved more than Rs 1.97 lakh crore in foreign exchange and replaced about 316 lakh tonnes of crude oil. In 2025-26 the three oil companies blended 1,134 crore litres of ethanol into about 5,673 crore litres of petrol sold, ministry data show.

The programme has faced complaints from some motorists about lower mileage and wear in older vehicles, which the ministry has disputed. The dispute also comes as Mr Gandhi and the Congress are attacking the Centre on several fronts, including the special revision of electoral rolls and a proposal to use voter ID rather than Aadhaar for welfare payments.

## What happens next

The oil companies have asked for joint retesting. Whether Karnataka agrees, and whether the Centre or the Bureau of Indian Standards orders its own tests, will decide whether the dispute moves from politics to evidence.
